newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - Oct 10.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - Oct 10.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
DAILY TELEGRAPH
-- HOUSE PRICE GAP BEGINS TO OPEN

According to figures from the Halifax Building Society, a North-South divide in house prices is emerging, with London property leading the boom with a ten per cent rise. The last time the Halifax index recorded double-digit house price inflation in any region was six years ago. All regions recorded yearly increases but prices in Scotland, Yorkshire and Humberside, East Anglia and the West Midlands were static, or fell over the third quarter.
-- HAWAII ISLE LINK IN PETER YOUNG PROBE

Morgan Grenfell investigators have uncovered a Luxembourg holding company, Litia Produktion, set up by disgraced fund manager Peter Young, which appears to have unusual links with a Bermuda-based company whose purpose is to invest in business opportunities in the Hawaiian island of Maui. In January, Maui USA received a loan of 3.4 million stg from Morgan Grenfell Asset Management, the bulk of which was invested in Kahana Ridge, a residential development in West Maui.
-- DIRECTOR OF TRAIN GROUP GOT SIX MILLION STG IN SECRET DEAL

Ian Cairns, the former commercial director of train leasing company Porterbrook, made 6.3 million stg from its takeover by Stagecoach after negotiating a secret deal with the company. His 80,000 shares would have netted him 12.7 million stg in cash and shares under the terms of Stagecoach's 159 stg-a-share offer. Porterbrook's articles of association stated that shareholders leaving the company had to sell back all their shares for a "fair value" price unless they obtained special dispensation. However, after negotiations with Porterbrook's remuneration committee Mr Cairns was allowed to keep 40,000 shares to sell on to Stagecoach.
THE TIMES
-- HOMES SLOWDOWN FUELS CLARKE STANCE ON RATES

Chancellor Kenneth Clarke has continued to ignore warnings from the Bank of England that interest rates should be raised. Last month's monetary meeting saw the Chancellor arguing that prices data remained extremely good and that sterling had strengthened since the last meeting. Governor of the Bank of England Eddie George said that the longer a rate rise was delayed the sharper it would need to be and that growing domestic demand put the Government's inflation target at risk.
-- TAX AND CUSTOMS STAFF CRITICISED

According to a report published by the independent financial adjudicator, Elizabeth Filkin, taxmen are incompetent, insensitive and indifferent, while Customs officials are overbearing and heavy-handed when questioning travellers. The report confirmed that complaining to the tax office can be a frustrating and time-consuming business. The Inland Revenue's attitude has led to frustration and fear, huge bills and unnecessary work for tax-payers.
-- ROVER PLANT WAITS ON 60 MILLION STG SUBSIDY

The BMW subsidiary Rover is close to securing a 60 million stg government subsidy to build an engine plant in the Midlands, between Coventry and Birmingham. The 500 million stg investment by the company could create 2,000 jobs. The investment could also go to Australia, where BMW already has a high-tech plant. By the beginning of the next decade Rover hopes to build 400,000 engines a year in Britain.
THE GUARDIAN
-- GAS COMPETITION IN CHAOS

The Government's experiment with gas competition appears to be descending into chaos as a flood of complaints from customers in the South-west has led to an emergency investigation by consumer watchdogs. The inquiry concerns customers who have received threatening letters from debt collectors acting for British Gas, even though they owe the company nothing. The customers are among those who switched to new suppliers when the domestic gas market in the region was opened up to competition earlier this year. Consumer groups blame the problems on computer systems at British Gas.
-- REUTERS UNFAZED BY CLARKE ATTACK

The ruling by Chancellor Kenneth Clarke on share buy-backs has been shrugged off by media group Reuters, which still hopes to return part of its 860 million stg cash pile to shareholders. Reuters chief executive Peter Job said the company would wait until after the Finance Bill before deciding what steps to take next. Store chain Allders, which was hoping to win approval for a share consolidation, had to abandon its plans.
-- MURDOCH TO SUE IN CLASH OF THE CABLE NEWS TITANS

Rupert Murdoch's News Corporation has said it is suing Time Warner for allegedly reneging on an agreement to carry the new Fox News Channel on its US cable systems. News Corp have said it would seek a permanent injunction against Time Warner's acquisition of Turner Broadcasting, which was expected to receive shareholders' approval today. The suit will allege anti-trust violations between Time Warner and Turner to block the Fox News Channel. The lawsuit has little chance of success because the deal has won Federal Trade Commission approval.
THE INDEPENDENT
-- CABLE AND WIRELESS STEPS IN TO SIGN UP GERMAN PARTNER

Cable and Wireless is set to join forces with RWE, the German utility, with the intention of developing its German telecoms business. Agreement was reached following the collapse of British Telecom's alliance with the German utility. C and W are set to own 22.5 per cent of a joint venture, grouping Vebacom, C and W's partnership with Veba, and RWE's telecoms operations. The new network will have a service and network company, which will operate separately.
-- BRITISH ENERGY UNDER FIRE OVER JOBS CUTS

Labour's energy spokesman, John Battle, called on Ian Lang, the President of the Board of Trade, to apologise at the Conservative Party conference for the privatisation of nuclear generator, British Energy, which has confirmed it is to cut 1,460 jobs. The cuts come three months after its stock market flotation. A British Energy spokesperson said there was no question of safety standards being compromised.
-- TEBITT TELLS COURT OF 'AGEISM'

Lord Tebbitt, former Conservative Party chairman, has told the High Court that a "cult of ageism" in Britain was making it difficult for top executives over the age of 55 to find work. He was giving evidence for corporate trouble shooter John Clark in his three million stg compensation claim for loss of his post as chief executive of BET, the business services group, after it was taken over by Rentokil.
